aeo.what_is: A chronic pattern of mood ups and downs that are milder than bipolar episodes but never fully stable.

content.temporal_criteria: Symptoms must be present for at least two years in adults (one year in children and adolescents) with no symptom-free period longer than two consecutive months. The mood fluctuations are chronic and persistent, without meeting full criteria for manic, hypomanic, or major depressive episodes during this time.

confused_with: Bipolar II Disorder — cyclothymia involves subthreshold symptoms that never reach full hypomanic or major depressive episode criteria, while Bipolar II includes distinct episodes meeting full diagnostic thresholds.

Borderline Personality Disorder — BPD mood shifts are rapid, reactive to interpersonal events, and accompanied by identity disturbance and fear of abandonment, while cyclothymic mood changes are more spontaneous and chronic without the interpersonal focus.
Major Depressive Disorder — MDD involves discrete depressive episodes with periods of normal mood in between, whereas cyclothymia features chronic fluctuating mood without sustained normal periods.
ADHD — ADHD symptoms are stable and lifelong with consistent inattention/hyperactivity, while cyclothymia involves mood-driven energy and motivation changes that fluctuate over days to weeks.
Normal mood variability — everyone has mood fluctuations, but cyclothymia involves persistent, impairing patterns over years that disrupt relationships, work, and self-esteem.
misdiagnosis_explained.clarifying_factors: Two years of mood charting showing persistent fluctuations without symptom-free periods longer than two months; collateral history confirming chronicity; ruling out full mood episodes; assessing functional impairment from the chronic instability; distinguishing spontaneous cycling from reactive emotional dysregulation.
misdiagnosis_explained.timeline_differences: Personality disorders and ADHD are stable patterns present since adolescence/early adulthood. Bipolar II has distinct episodes with clear onset and offset. Cyclothymia is chronic with fluctuating intensity but never reaching full episode thresholds. MDD has discrete episodes separated by wellness.
misdiagnosis_explained.impairment_differences: Full mood episodes (MDD, Bipolar II) cause more severe acute impairment. Cyclothymia causes chronic low-grade impairment from never having sustained stability—relationships strain, work is inconsistent, and self-esteem suffers from the unpredictability.

description.overview: Cyclothymic Disorder is a chronic mood disorder characterized by numerous periods of hypomanic symptoms and periods of depressive symptoms that do not meet full criteria for a hypomanic, manic, or major depressive episode. Symptoms persist for at least 2 years in adults (1 year in children/adolescents) with no symptom-free period longer than 2 months.
what_it_can_look_like_in_real_life: A 25-year-old describes feeling 'up and down all the time'—some days she's energized, talkative, and stays up late working on projects, other days she's low-energy, withdrawn, and doubts herself. Neither extreme is severe enough to meet full diagnostic criteria, but the pattern has been constant for three years.

A 32-year-old can't hold a job for more than a year because his mood and energy fluctuate unpredictably. Coworkers notice he's sometimes enthusiastic and productive, other times irritable and disengaged. He's never had full mania or deep depression, but he's never felt stable either.

A 19-year-old college student alternates between weeks of high social activity, needing less sleep, and feeling confident, and weeks of low motivation, oversleeping, and avoiding friends. Her roommates say she's 'moody,' but neither phase disrupts her functioning severely—it just never stops cycling.

A 40-year-old realizes she's been on this 'roller coaster' since her twenties: good days where she's chatty and starts new hobbies, followed by down days where she's quiet and loses interest. Friends describe her as unpredictable, and she's struggled with relationships because of it.

A 28-year-old seeks help because he's 'never just OK.' He has brief stretches of high energy and spending, then drops into periods of low mood and fatigue. Neither is severe enough to be considered bipolar, but the constant cycling has made it hard to maintain routines or plan his life.
common_reactions_to_diagnosis: Relief that the chronic ups and downs have a name and aren't just a character flaw.
Confusion about whether it's 'serious enough' to need treatment since the extremes aren't as severe as bipolar disorder.
Frustration that it's been dismissed as 'just moodiness' for years.
Worry that it might progress to Bipolar I or II.
Validation that the instability is real and not something they're imagining.
Hope that treatment can bring stability they've never experienced.

content.diagnostic_criteria: A. ≥2 years (≥1 year for youth) of numerous periods of hypomanic symptoms and depressive symptoms that do not meet criteria for hypomanic/manic or major depressive episode. B. Symptoms present for at least half the time with no more than 2 consecutive months symptom-free. C. Criteria for major depressive, manic, or hypomanic episode never met. D. Symptoms are not better explained by another mental disorder, substance, or medical condition. E. Cause clinically significant distress or impairment.
content.prevalence: Lifetime prevalence estimated at 0.4–1%, but often underrecognized or misdiagnosed as personality disorder or recurrent depression.
content.age_of_onset: Usually adolescence or early adulthood; insidious onset with chronic course.
content.prognosis: Chronic course with risk of progression to Bipolar I or II Disorder (15–50%). Early recognition and mood stabilization reduce functional impairment and risk behaviors.

circuitry: Abnormal connectivity between prefrontal cortex and limbic regions (amygdala, hippocampus) leading to emotion regulation difficulties.
Dysregulation in reward circuits and circadian systems.
neurochemistry: Alterations in dopamine, serotonin, and norepinephrine signaling contributing to mood lability.
neurobiology.genetic_environmental: Family history of bipolar spectrum disorders increases risk; stress, sleep disruption, and substance use exacerbate cycling.

history_psychosocial: Longitudinal mood charting to identify chronic fluctuations and absence of full mood episodes.
Collateral history from family/friends to identify subthreshold hypomanic behaviors.
medical_assessment: Rule out thyroid dysfunction, seizure disorders, and substance effects.
Consider medication review for agents that may mimic mood cycling.
standardized_measures: Mood Disorder Questionnaire (MDQ) for screening; Hypomania Checklist (HCL-32); PHQ-9 for depressive symptoms.
Daily mood charting to monitor fluctuations.
risk_stratification: Assess for suicidality, impulsivity, and substance use given mood instability.
Evaluate psychosocial impact across work, school, and relationships.
differential_diagnosis: Bipolar II Disorder (full hypomanic episodes present).
Borderline Personality Disorder (affective reactivity to interpersonal stress rather than spontaneous mood shifts).
Recurrent Major Depressive Disorder (no hypomanic symptoms).
ADHD (persistent attentional issues without clear episodicity).
evaluation.team_and_process: Collaboration between psychiatry, psychotherapy, and primary care; psychoeducation for patient and family; regular monitoring.

associated_features: Mood instability leading to unstable relationships and inconsistent work performance

severity_levels.mild: Symptoms present but manageable with minimal functional impairment.
severity_levels.moderate: Frequent fluctuations causing noticeable work, academic, or interpersonal impact.
severity_levels.severe: Persistent cycling with significant impairment and high comorbidity.

biological: Family history of bipolar spectrum disorders

impact_on_life.school_work: Inconsistent productivity and difficulty sustaining long-term projects.
impact_on_life.social: Relationship instability due to unpredictable mood changes.
impact_on_life.medical: Potential for sleep disorders, metabolic concerns from medications.

medications: Mood stabilizers: lithium, lamotrigine, valproate (for significant cycling).
Atypical antipsychotics: quetiapine, lurasidone, cariprazine for mood stabilization.
Antidepressants generally avoided as monotherapy due to risk of switching.
Regular monitoring for side effects and serum levels where applicable.
psychotherapy: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) focusing on emotion regulation.
Interpersonal and Social Rhythm Therapy (IPSRT) to stabilize routines.
Psychoeducation for patient and family on early warning signs.
lifestyle_interventions: Consistent sleep–wake schedule; avoid shift work.
Exercise, healthy diet, and stress management techniques.
Limit alcohol and avoid recreational drugs.
care_coordination: Collaborative care between psychiatry and primary care.
Involvement of family or trusted supports for monitoring.

treatment_goals: Reduce frequency and intensity of mood fluctuations.
Prevent progression to Bipolar I or II Disorder.
Improve functioning and quality of life.
Enhance coping skills and stress resilience.
missed_diagnosis_factors: Symptoms dismissed as 'moodiness' or personality traits.
Focus on depressive symptoms without probing for hypomanic periods.
Lack of longitudinal history or mood charting.
overdiagnosis_factors: Labeling situational mood swings as cyclothymia without chronicity.
Confusing affective instability from borderline personality disorder with spontaneous cycling.
Overinterpretation of mood questionnaires without confirming duration and impairment.
warning_signs: Notable drop in mood or energy without clear trigger.

adolescence: Mood changes may be attributed to puberty; school performance may fluctuate.
young_adulthood: Career and relationship instability common; early intervention crucial.
midlife_older_adults: Cycling may become less intense but more persistent; comorbid medical issues may complicate treatment.

first_person_statements: I've never known what 'stable' feels like—I'm always either a little up or a little down, never just steady.
People think I'm dramatic or inconsistent, but it's not a choice. My mood just swings and I can't predict it.
I've had this my whole adult life. I didn't realize it was a disorder until I started tracking my mood and saw the pattern.
The hardest part is that it's chronic. It's not one bad episode I can recover from—it's constant, and I never get a break.
Relationships are tough because I'm not the same person week to week. Partners get frustrated when they can't predict how I'll be.
Treatment helped me realize stability is possible. I didn't know life could feel less chaotic.

comparisons: It's like living on a never-ending seesaw that tilts gently up and down, never settling in the middle, and you can't step off.
Imagine your mood is a radio that constantly shifts between stations—never loud enough to be alarming, but never tuned in clearly either.
Think of it as a milder, chronic version of bipolar disorder: the highs and lows are less extreme, but they never stop, and that relentlessness wears you down.
It's like emotional weather that's always changing—sometimes sunny, sometimes cloudy—but you never get a stretch of clear, predictable days.

faqs.question: How is cyclothymic disorder different from Bipolar II?
faqs.answer: Cyclothymia involves chronic, subthreshold mood fluctuations that never meet full criteria for hypomanic or major depressive episodes. Bipolar II includes distinct episodes of full hypomania and major depression. Cyclothymia is milder but more persistent.

faqs.question: Can cyclothymia turn into bipolar disorder?
faqs.answer: Yes. About 15–50% of people with cyclothymic disorder eventually experience a full manic, hypomanic, or major depressive episode, at which point the diagnosis changes to Bipolar I or II. Early treatment may reduce this risk.

faqs.question: Is cyclothymia serious if the mood swings aren't extreme?
faqs.answer: Yes. The chronic instability can significantly impair relationships, work, and quality of life. People often struggle with self-esteem, inconsistent performance, and unpredictability. The cumulative impact over years can be substantial.

faqs.question: How long do the mood shifts last in cyclothymia?
faqs.answer: Mood shifts vary but typically last days to weeks, with frequent alternation. Unlike Bipolar II, which has distinct episodes with clear start and end points, cyclothymia features a more fluid, chronic pattern.

faqs.question: Do I need treatment if my symptoms are mild?
faqs.answer: If the symptoms cause distress or functional impairment, treatment is beneficial. Mood stabilizers, psychotherapy, and lifestyle changes can reduce fluctuations, improve functioning, and potentially prevent progression to full bipolar disorder.

faqs.question: Can therapy alone treat cyclothymia?
faqs.answer: Therapy (especially CBT and IPSRT) is very helpful for managing symptoms, stabilizing routines, and improving coping. Some people may need medication (mood stabilizers or atypicals) in addition, especially if impairment is significant or symptoms worsen.

faqs.question: What triggers the mood shifts in cyclothymia?
faqs.answer: Triggers can include sleep disruption, stress, substance use, and seasonal changes, but shifts often occur spontaneously without clear triggers. Maintaining consistent routines and sleep helps reduce variability.

faqs.question: Is cyclothymia genetic?
faqs.answer: Yes. Family history of bipolar disorder and major depression increases risk. Cyclothymia has a hereditary component, though environmental factors (stress, substance use) also play a role.

faqs.question: Can I work or go to school with cyclothymia?
faqs.answer: Yes. Many people with cyclothymia work and study successfully, though the instability can be challenging. Treatment, accommodations (flexible schedules, understanding supervisors), and consistent routines help maintain functioning.

faqs.question: How is cyclothymia diagnosed?
faqs.answer: Diagnosis requires prospective mood tracking over time to confirm at least two years (one year in youth) of chronic fluctuations without symptom-free periods longer than two months, and without meeting full episode criteria. A detailed clinical interview and collateral history are essential.

faqs.question: Will mood stabilizers flatten my mood completely?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. The goal is to reduce the extremes and increase stability, allowing you to experience normal emotions without the disruptive cycling. Finding the right medication and dose is a collaborative process.

faqs.question: Can substance use cause cyclothymia?
faqs.answer: Substance use doesn't cause cyclothymia, but stimulants, alcohol, and cannabis can worsen mood instability and make it harder to diagnose. Addressing substance use is an important part of treatment.

faqs.question: What's the difference between cyclothymia and just being moody?
faqs.answer: Everyone has mood variability. Cyclothymia involves persistent, impairing fluctuations over years that affect work, relationships, and self-esteem. It's chronic, not situational, and meets specific diagnostic criteria.

faqs.question: Can cyclothymia improve with age?
faqs.answer: Some people experience milder fluctuations with age, especially with consistent treatment and stable routines. However, without treatment, symptoms often persist or worsen, and the risk of progression to bipolar disorder remains.

faqs.question: Should I track my mood?
faqs.answer: Yes. Daily mood tracking helps you and your treatment team identify patterns, triggers, and early warning signs. It's one of the most useful tools for managing cyclothymia.

real_life_examples.person: A 19-year-old college student noticed she'd been alternating between periods of high energy, increased socializing, and needing little sleep, and times of low motivation, withdrawal, and fatigue for the past two years. Neither phase was severe enough to meet full episode criteria. Her therapist diagnosed cyclothymic disorder and started her on lamotrigine and IPSRT. Mood charting helped her stabilize routines, and she's now managing her classes with much less volatility.

A 35-year-old graphic designer sought help after years of job instability. He described lifelong 'ups and downs'—some weeks he'd work late, feel creative and confident, other weeks he'd struggle to start projects and feel unmotivated. Prospective mood tracking confirmed chronic subthreshold cycling. Lithium and CBT reduced the extremes, and he's maintained steady employment for two years.

A 28-year-old noticed that for at least three years, she'd never felt 'just OK.' She'd have stretches of chattiness, impulsive spending, and staying up late, followed by days of low energy and self-doubt. Her doctor diagnosed cyclothymic disorder and started quetiapine. With therapy and sleep hygiene, her mood stabilized, and her partner reported she was 'more predictable and easier to connect with.'

A 24-year-old with a family history of bipolar disorder sought evaluation after friends noticed his mood was 'always changing.' Mood charting over two months confirmed chronic, subthreshold fluctuations. His psychiatrist explained the risk of progression and started lamotrigine prophylactically. He now uses a mood app, maintains strict sleep routines, and has remained stable without full episodes.

content.when_to_seek_help: Seek evaluation if mood changes are persistent, disruptive, or associated with risky behavior, even if they do not meet criteria for major mood episodes.

positive_factors: Strong insight and adherence to treatment
